title: Trump: National Intelligence says Congress will not be allowed briefings on election interference
description_short: Trump: National Intelligence says Congress will not be allowed briefings on election interference
description_medium: On August 29, 2020, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence told congressional intelligence committees it would replace in-person election-security briefings with written updates. The change meant members could no longer ask follow-up questions directly to intelligence officials. Former DNI James Clapper warned that written reports removed probing back-and-forth at a time when lawmakers were preparing for foreign interference in the election.
description_long: The Office of the Director of National Intelligence notified congressional intelligence committees that it would stop providing in-person briefings on election security and instead send written updates. Those meetings had allowed lawmakers to ask officials follow-up questions about confusing or incomplete information. Former Director of National Intelligence James Clapper warned that written reports would remove that exchange and could make officials less likely to disclose sensitive information about foreign interference. The Justice, Homeland Security, and Defense departments were expected to continue their own briefings, but the timeline noted that several of their leaders had repeated claims made by President Donald Trump. The change came in the run-up to the 2020 election, when federal agencies were assessing attempts by foreign governments to influence the vote. The entry documents a change in how the intelligence community communicated with Congress, rather than a finding that election interference did or did not occur. It also records concern from former officials that limiting questions could reduce oversight and leave legislators with less ability to probe what agencies knew. The decision mattered because briefings were a direct channel between national security officials and elected representatives during an active election-security debate.
organization_tags: Office of the Director of National Intelligence

title: Trump: Punishing states that voted against him, Trump cancels $18 billion infrastructure project
description_short: Trump: Punishing states that voted against him, Trump cancels $18 billion infrastructure project
description_medium: On October 1, 2025, the Trump administration froze roughly $18 billion for two major New York City infrastructure projects and about $8 billion for green-energy projects across 16 states. Officials cited concerns about contracting during the government shutdown. Later court documents, as summarized by the timeline, indicated that hundreds of terminated energy grants were concentrated in states that voted for Kamala Harris and were not cancelled for programmatic or cost reasons.
description_long: The funding freeze affected two large New York City transportation projects: the Second Avenue subway expansion and new commuter rail tunnels beneath the Hudson River. The timeline placed their combined $18 billion in federal funding alongside a separate freeze of about $8 billion for green-energy projects in 16 states, including California and Illinois. The administration cited concerns about allegedly discriminatory contracting by New York, while state transportation officials said the explanation threatened projects intended to relieve major travel bottlenecks. The timeline also reports that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy had previously told Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand funding would continue. Later court documents described in the source concerned 284 energy grants terminated in states that voted for Kamala Harris; an Energy Department lawyer reportedly acknowledged that, with one exception, those grants were not selected for programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction, or performance reasons. That later filing adds evidence relevant to claims of political retaliation, but it is distinct from the initial October announcement and does not by itself resolve every legal question about the New York projects. The entry records the funding decisions, the administration’s stated justification, and the subsequent court-filed account of grant terminations.

title: Trump: Jared Kushner & Trump Campaign fight Fox News for giving Arizona to Biden
description_short: Trump: Jared Kushner & Trump Campaign fight Fox News for giving Arizona to Biden
description_medium: After Fox News projected Joe Biden would win Arizona on election night in 2020, Trump campaign adviser Jared Kushner contacted Fox owner Rupert Murdoch and asked him to retract the call. Campaign adviser Jason Miller was also reported to have pressed the network. Kushner later sought a “James Baker-like” figure to lead efforts to contest vote counts in several states.
description_long: Fox News projected that Joe Biden had won Arizona late on election night, November 3, 2020. The following day, Jared Kushner, then a senior Trump campaign adviser, privately contacted Rupert Murdoch, whose companies owned Fox News and the New York Post, and asked him to have the network retract its call. Campaign adviser Jason Miller was also reported to have urged Fox to reverse the projection. The request came while the Trump campaign was challenging vote counts in multiple states after the election. Kushner later looked for a person he described as a “James Baker-like” figure to oversee the campaign’s effort, invoking the role Baker had played in the 2000 Florida recount. The episode shows the campaign seeking intervention from a media owner after a network projected a state for Biden, while also preparing a broader contest over the results. The supplied account does not say that Murdoch or Fox withdrew the Arizona projection. This entry records the reported private request and the campaign’s parallel search for a recount strategist; it does not treat a request to retract a call as evidence that the network changed its decision.

title: Trump Sells Advanced F-35 Fighter Jets to UAE as Abraham Accords Side Deal
description_short: Trump Sells Advanced F-35 Fighter Jets to UAE as Abraham Accords Side Deal
description_medium: In November 2020, the Trump administration advanced a proposed arms package for the United Arab Emirates that included up to 50 F-35 stealth fighters, armed drones, and other weapons, with an estimated value of $23 billion. The sale followed the UAE-Israel Abraham Accords and raised concerns about Israel’s U.S.-backed qualitative military edge. The Biden administration later paused the transaction for review; the aircraft were not delivered as part of this announcement.
description_long: The Trump administration agreed to pursue a sale of up to 50 advanced F-35 fighters to the United Arab Emirates, along with armed drones and other weapons, in a package valued at about $23 billion. The proposed sale followed the UAE’s normalization agreement with Israel, known as the Abraham Accords, and was presented as part of the diplomatic opening. It raised concerns in Israel because longstanding U.S. policy had sought to preserve Israel’s qualitative military edge over neighboring states. Israeli officials reportedly lobbied privately against the arms transfer even as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu publicly praised the accords. The Biden administration later paused the sale for review of its security and regional-stability implications. The entry concerns the proposed transfer and the debate around it; it does not claim the aircraft were delivered or that the sale proceeded as initially announced. Critics argued that advanced U.S. weapons were being offered as a diplomatic incentive, while supporters viewed the package within a broader regional realignment. The decision involved arms control, U.S. commitments to Israel, and the UAE-Israel normalization process, making the timing and terms politically consequential beyond the commercial value of the deal.

title: Trump Asks Intelligence Chiefs to Publicly Deny Russia Investigation
description_short: Trump Asks Intelligence Chiefs to Publicly Deny Russia Investigation
description_medium: In 2017, President Trump reportedly asked intelligence chiefs Dan Coats and Mike Rogers to publicly state that there was no evidence of collusion between his campaign and Russia. The requests came while the FBI was conducting a counterintelligence investigation. Coats and Rogers declined, and contemporaneous accounts said they documented their conversations. Coats later testified under oath that Trump had made such requests.
description_long: The supplied account describes conversations in March and May 2017 in which Trump asked Director of National Intelligence Dan Coats and NSA Director Mike Rogers to publicly deny evidence of collusion between the Trump campaign and Russia. The requests came after the FBI investigation became public and while it remained ongoing. Coats and Rogers did not issue the requested statements. Reporting cited in the entry said both officials recorded the conversations in contemporaneous memoranda, and Coats later testified under oath that Trump had asked him to make a public statement about the investigation. The episode raised concern that the president was asking senior intelligence leaders to weigh in publicly on an active counterintelligence inquiry involving his campaign. The description reports the requests and officials’ responses rather than asserting a legal conclusion about obstruction. It also distinguishes an intelligence official’s assessment from the public statement Trump sought: the issue was not simply what the agencies knew, but pressure to use their authority to shape public understanding of the investigation. The event is documented through reporting and later testimony, not through a public finding that the request changed the investigation’s outcome.

title: ICE Ends 'Sensitive Locations' Protections: Arrests at Churches, Schools, Hospitals
description_short: ICE Ends 'Sensitive Locations' Protections: Arrests at Churches, Schools, Hospitals
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Acting Homeland Security Secretary Benjamine Huffman rescinded the policy limiting immigration arrests at schools, hospitals, churches, and other sensitive locations. A later ICE memo gave officers case-by-case discretion. In March, a federal court restored protections for certain houses of worship without a valid warrant, while the broader protections for schools and hospitals remained withdrawn.
description_long: Acting Homeland Security Secretary Benjamine Huffman rescinded the 2011 sensitive-locations policy on January 20, 2025. That policy had generally limited Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection from making immigration arrests at schools, hospitals, churches, and similar sites. An ICE memo issued later in January renamed the change “Common Sense Enforcement Actions” and allowed field officers to decide case by case, without categorical protections for those venues. The policy shift caused concern in immigrant communities; the supplied account says some families pulled children from school. In March 2025, a federal court issued an injunction requiring ICE to follow the old guidance at roughly 1,400 houses of worship in 36 states when officers lacked a valid warrant. That order did not restore the same protections to schools, hospitals, or all other sensitive locations. The entry documents both the rescission and the narrower court intervention, rather than suggesting the injunction restored the full prior policy nationwide. The change affected where immigration enforcement could occur and raised questions about access to education, health care, and worship for people concerned about arrest or detention.

title: Trump Claims He Invented the Word 'Prime' (as in Prime the Pump)
description_short: Trump Claims He Invented the Word 'Prime' (as in Prime the Pump)
description_medium: During a May 2017 interview with The Economist, Donald Trump said he had never heard the phrase “prime the pump” before and believed he had coined it. He asked the interviewer to confirm that it was new. Merriam-Webster noted that the expression had appeared in print as early as 1933, decades before the interview.
description_long: In an interview with The Economist published May 11, 2017, Trump discussed the expression “prime the pump,” a phrase used for government spending intended to stimulate economic activity. He said he had not heard it before and claimed he had come up with it only days earlier. Trump pressed the interviewer to confirm that the expression was new. Merriam-Webster responded publicly that the phrase had been used since at least 1933, well before Trump’s claim. The exchange became a small but widely repeated example of Trump asserting personal credit for a familiar expression. The source material supports the contrast between his statement and the documented history of the phrase; it does not establish whether he knowingly misrepresented its origin or genuinely did not know it was longstanding. The event is narrower than a policy dispute: it records a claim made in an interview and a dictionary’s correction. Its relevance is the president’s public handling of basic economic language while promoting an economic argument, and the ease with which a direct historical reference contradicted the claim of invention.

title: Trump Promotes MyPillow CEO Mike Lindell's Voting Machine Theories (2021)
description_short: Trump Promotes MyPillow CEO Mike Lindell's Voting Machine Theories (2021)
description_medium: In January 2021, Trump hosted MyPillow CEO Mike Lindell at the White House and later promoted Lindell’s claims that voting machines had been hacked to change the 2020 election result. Lindell’s “Absolute Proof” documentary repeated the allegations, and Dominion Voting Systems sued him for defamation. At an August cyber symposium, experts who reviewed Lindell’s purported data described it as unreliable.
description_long: Mike Lindell, chief executive of MyPillow, promoted claims that voting machines had been hacked by China or other foreign actors to change the 2020 election outcome. Trump hosted Lindell at the White House in January 2021 and later amplified his allegations to a large online audience. Lindell released a documentary, “Absolute Proof,” presenting the claims. Dominion Voting Systems filed a $1.3 billion defamation lawsuit against him over statements about the company’s machines. Lindell continued to appear at events associated with Trump, including an August 2021 “Cyber Symposium” where he promised to show proof of hacking. Experts who attended said the data he presented did not substantiate the claims. The entry records the relationship between the two men and Trump’s promotion of allegations about election technology after the 2020 result had been certified. The source linked for the entry documents Lindell’s White House visit; the supplied synopsis provides the later context about the documentary, lawsuit, and symposium. These were claims about election systems, not verified evidence that votes had been changed. Dominion’s lawsuit also remained a legal allegation at the time described, not a judgment on the merits in this entry.

title: Trump Amplifies Russian Disinformation About Biden Family in Ukraine (2020)
description_short: Trump Amplifies Russian Disinformation About Biden Family in Ukraine (2020)
description_medium: In October 2020, Trump and allies promoted allegations about the Biden family based on material from Ukrainian politician Andrii Derkach, whom the Treasury Department had identified as a Russian intelligence asset. U.S. intelligence officials warned that the material was part of a Russian influence effort. The FBI found no evidence of criminal wrongdoing by Joe or Hunter Biden in the Ukraine business dealings described in the supplied account.
description_long: In the final weeks of the 2020 campaign, Trump and allies including Rudy Giuliani and Sen. Ron Johnson circulated material from Ukrainian politician Andrii Derkach alleging corrupt financial dealings by the Biden family in Ukraine. The Treasury Department had identified Derkach as a Russian intelligence asset, and U.S. intelligence officials warned the Senate that the material was part of an active Russian influence operation. Trump promoted the claims, including during the presidential debates. The supplied account says an FBI investigation found no evidence of criminal wrongdoing by Joe or Hunter Biden related to their Ukraine business dealings. It also notes that the Senate Intelligence Committee had previously criticized Trump’s 2019 pressure on Ukraine to investigate political opponents. The episode involved two distinct issues: whether the Biden family committed crimes, for which the account reports no supporting FBI evidence, and the use of material linked by U.S. officials to a foreign influence operation in domestic campaigning. The entry describes the allegations as claims promoted by Trump and his allies, not as established facts. It records how material from an identified Russian influence effort entered the campaign debate and how U.S. officials warned lawmakers about its provenance.

title: Department of Education Gutted 50%, Declared 'Final Mission'
description_short: Department of Education Gutted 50%, Declared 'Final Mission'
description_medium: On March 11, 2025, the Department of Education announced a reduction in force affecting nearly half its workforce. The department said more than 1,300 positions would be cut and about 600 employees had already accepted voluntary resignations, leaving roughly 2,183 staff. Secretary Linda McMahon presented the cuts as part of Trump’s effort to shrink the department, which Congress had not voted to abolish.
description_long: The Department of Education announced a large reduction in force on March 11, 2025, affecting nearly half of its 4,133-person workforce. The supplied account says more than 1,300 positions were eliminated and about 600 staff members had already accepted voluntary resignations, leaving roughly 2,183 employees. The department’s “Final Mission” notice said affected employees would be placed on paid administrative leave beginning March 21 and remain on payroll through June 9. Government Accountability Office data later showed a workforce decline of more than 45 percent, the largest among major federal agencies that year. The department oversees federal student loans, Pell Grants, and civil-rights enforcement in schools, so the staffing reductions could affect its ability to administer those responsibilities. Secretary Linda McMahon described the cuts as fulfilling Trump’s pledge to close the department, although Congress had not passed legislation abolishing it. The event was a substantial administrative downsizing, not a formal closure of the department. The entry distinguishes the administration’s stated goal from the legal step that would be required to eliminate a federal agency and records the immediate reduction in staffing and the programs that office manages.
